summary: This informational memo from AT&T/Neda specifies the Efficient Short Remote Operations protocol: its service model, notation and protocol, in version 1.2.

eli5.summary: A quick way for one computer to ask another to do a small job and tell it the result.

questions: when should i use esro instead of rpc
how does esro save bandwidth on wireless
what is the difference between 2-way and 3-way handshake
subtitle: Lightweight remote procedure calls optimized for wireless and connectionless networks.

tldr.problem: Remote Procedure Call systems typically require connection setup overhead that wastes battery and bandwidth on wireless networks. Existing RPC mechanisms like ONC RPC are designed for larger, more reliable messages.
tldr.mechanism: ESRO provides a connectionless RPC protocol layered on UDP with a focus on minimal overhead. It supports both reliable 3-way handshakes and fast 2-way handshakes, with optional segmentation and message concatenation to handle larger operations.
tldr.outcome: Applications can invoke operations on remote machines with minimal protocol machinery, trading certainty in some cases for speed and efficiency. It was designed with wireless networks like CDPD in mind.

sections.title: What is ESRO?
sections.content:
ESRO stands for Efficient Short Remote Operations. It is a protocol that lets one program ask another program on the network to do something and report back the result. Unlike traditional Remote Procedure Call (RPC) systems, ESRO is designed from the ground up for efficiency, with special attention to wireless networks where every byte sent and every millisecond matters.

The key difference from standard RPC is that ESRO runs over UDP, a connectionless transport, and keeps its headers and messages small. It also lets applications choose between speed and reliability: the protocol supports a quick 2-way handshake for operations where some loss is acceptable, and a more careful 3-way handshake when results must be confirmed.
sections.eli5: ESRO is a way to ask a computer on the Internet to do a job and get back the answer, but designed to be really fast and not use much data.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
An ESRO operation involves two roles: the invoker (the client asking for work) and the performer (the server doing the work). The invoker sends an INVOKE message containing the operation number, arguments, and the performer's address. The performer receives it, does the work, and sends back either a RESULT message (if successful) or an ERROR message (if something went wrong).

Each operation gets a unique invoke ID, which lets both sides match replies to requests even when multiple operations are in flight at once. The protocol is asynchronous by default, so the invoker does not have to wait for a reply before sending the next request.
sections.eli5: You write what job you want done on a postcard, mail it, and the other computer mails you back a postcard with the answer.

sections.title: Message Types and Reliability Choices
sections.content:
ESRO defines several Protocol Data Units (PDUs). The main ones are: ESRO-INVOKE (the request), ESRO-RESULT (successful reply), ESRO-ERROR (failure reply), ESRO-ACK (acknowledging a result or error), and ESRO-FAILURE (telling the invoker the operation could not be delivered). Large operations can be split into ESRO-INVOKE-SEGMENTED and ESRO-RESULT-SEGMENTED PDUs, which the receiver reassembles.

The protocol offers two service modes. Acknowledged Result mode uses a 3-way handshake: the invoker sends INVOKE, the performer sends RESULT or ERROR, and the invoker sends back an ACK. This ensures the performer knows the invoker got the answer. Non-Acknowledged Result mode skips the final ACK: the performer sends RESULT or ERROR but does not expect confirmation. The invoker may never know if its result got through.
sections.eli5: The protocol lets you choose: either both sides confirm everything they got (slow but sure), or one side just sends what it knows and hopes the other got it (fast but risky).

sections.title: Efficiency Features
sections.content:
ESRO includes several features to reduce overhead on bandwidth-limited networks. Segmentation and Reassembly lets the protocol split large messages into smaller PDUs and put them back together at the receiver. Concatenation lets the protocol pack multiple small PDUs into one UDP datagram to reduce the number of packets sent.

Parameters like Source Port and Destination Port identify which application on each machine is invoking or performing the operation. The protocol also supports an encoding-type tag so the invoker and performer can agree on how to encode the operation arguments and results—for example, using XDR (External Data Representation) or other formats.
sections.eli5: To save space, ESRO can stuff multiple requests into one packet, or split one big request across several packets and put it back together on the other end.

sections.title: Uses and Status
sections.content:
The RFC names several early applications: efficient short message submission and delivery, credit card authorization, and white pages (directory) lookup. These are operations where the request and response are usually small and where latency matters more than having a full connection.

RFC 2188 is informational and not an Internet standard. The IESG noted that the protocol has not had IETF Working Group review and flagged potential scalability concerns for sites considering deployment. This reflects that ESRO was a vendor specification (AT&T/Neda) proposed to the IETF as an informational reference, not a standards-track protocol.
sections.eli5: ESRO was used for things like sending short messages quickly, checking credit cards, and looking up people in a phone book. It is not an official Internet standard but an informational reference.

left.title: Acknowledged Result
left.desc: INVOKE sent, RESULT/ERROR received, ACK sent back. Both sides confirm.

right.title: Non-Acknowledged Result
right.desc: INVOKE sent, RESULT/ERROR sent but no ACK required. Faster, less reliable.
